meters.label: Other users' invoices Bob can read (of 15)
Other users' invoices Bob can change (of 15)

frames.narration: Bob logs in and opens his invoice 1002. The API checks his token is valid, loads invoice 1002 and returns it. All is well.
Bob changes the id in the URL to 1003, which belongs to Alice. The handler only asks who the caller is, not whose the invoice is. It returns Alice's invoice.
With sequential ids Bob counts up. With no ownership checks he reads, changes and deletes all 15 invoices that are not his.
Random ids look like a fix: Bob cannot guess them. But the list, the search and the per-user endpoint show everyone's ids, and then every id works. Still 15 of 15.
The team adds checks to GET, PUT and DELETE. Changing and deleting stop: 0 of 15. But the PDF download, the bulk export and the lists have separate handlers with no check, so Bob still reads 15.
A central policy: every handler loads objects through one function that takes the caller, the action and the object. A new endpoint cannot skip it. Bob reaches 0 of 15 everywhere.

Lists need care: scope the query by the caller's account so only their rows are read. Fetching all rows and checking each one is safe but, on 100,000 invoices, reads all 100,000 and makes 100,000 policy calls instead of 1.
Finally, test as a second user: log in as Bob, request Alice's objects on every endpoint for read, change and delete, and expect not-found. The missed endpoint becomes a failing test, not a breach.
